mappings.note: Infers a centralised, bureaucratic state from the administrative detail in the Arthashastra and Indika. The inference is about administration, so LO-78 rather than the sources goal.
Dates a site from polished stone, a pillar with an animal capital and 3rd-century BCE pottery - reading archaeological evidence to place a period. The goal's own sources clause.
Weighs weak successors, provincial revolt and economic crisis as causes of imperial decline against a false one. Reasoning about the limits of imperial control, so LO-78.
Accepts guild autonomy and rejects the claim of constant royal interference - economic organisation and its relation to the state. Not LO-78, because the point is that rulers stayed out.

The keyed statement is that the Arthashastra sets out the saptanga, and the rejected one misstates its welfare principle. Statecraft content, so LO-78 rather than treating the text merely as a source.

Megasthenes' report that farmers were shielded from war so cultivation continued describes a practice of the state. Not CG-SST2: the source is named, but what is tested is the protection of agriculture.

'Emissary' is defined as someone sent on a diplomatic mission, and Ashoka's dispatch of them is an act of statecraft. Not LO-81, because the item defines the office, not the rise of the religion they carried.
Names 'empire' as many kingdoms under one central ruler - the structure of imperial authority. Not CG-SST2, because the specific outcome on how states were held together applies.
Names 'tributary' for a state that submits and pays. A device of imperial control, like the tribute items in the earlier batches.
Recall of a Sanskrit title for emperor. Filed with the imperial-authority vocabulary rather than with the general goal.
Names Pataliputra as the capital in the chapter's narrative frame. A place recall, not an administrative point.
Names one function of an empire - army, administration, law, trade regulation, resources. The administration outcome in its plainest form.
'Posterity' as future generations - the vocabulary of legacy. The short-answer twin of the MCQ on the same word.
Names guilds or shrenis. Economic history, and the guilds were self-governing rather than organs of the state.
Magadha as the mahajanapada behind the first empires - chronology and political geography. Not LO-78, since no measure of rule is asked.
Ajatashatru as an early Magadhan king. A dynastic recall, not an analysis of his administration.

Names the Buddha and Mahavira as contemporaries of Ajatashatru, which places the founders of two new religious movements in this period. Not CG-SST2, because a specific outcome covers religious movements.
The Nanda dynasty and its founder - dynastic recall under the goal.
Panini as the grammarian of the Nanda period. Intellectual history and a source for the age.
The Ashtadhyayi as Panini's work. A text recall, the sources clause of the goal.
Alexander as the Greek king who invaded the northwest. Narrative history; no administrative measure is asked.
Porus as Alexander's Indian opponent. A person-and-event recall like its MCQ twin.
Names satraps as provincial governors - an office of imperial administration. Not CG-SST2, because the term belongs to how an empire was run.
'Gymnosophists' as the Greek name for Indian sages. Cultural-contact history; no religious movement's origin is analysed, so LO-81 would not fit.
The Mauryas replacing the Nandas - dynastic succession. Not LO-78, since no policy or measure is at issue.
Chandragupta Maurya as founder of the empire. Dynastic recall, the short-answer twin of the earlier MCQ.
Kautilya as Chandragupta's mentor - a biographical link. The Arthashastra's content carries LO-78 elsewhere, but here only the relationship is asked.
The title of Kautilya's work. A text recall under the sources clause; the items about what the Arthashastra says were given LO-78.
Megasthenes as the Greek visitor to the Mauryan court - the origin of a key source.
'Indika' as Megasthenes' book, surviving only in excerpts. A source recall, and the survival note is itself about how historians work.
'Devanampiya' as Ashoka's self-title in the edicts. Imperial self-presentation, grouped with the other title items.
Brahmi as the script of most edicts. A fact about the sources, unlike the items on why Prakrit and Brahmi were chosen, which were read as administrative intent.
Empire against kingdom, defined through tributary territories under a central emperor. The structure of imperial rule, so LO-78.
Explains tribute as regular payment acknowledging overlordship - the working of imperial control.
Lists three things an emperor had to manage - army, administration and resources. The administration outcome stated directly.

Controlling trade routes for revenue, resources and communication across the empire is a measure of imperial control. Not CG-SST2, because the reasoning is about holding the state together rather than about commerce itself.
Defines guilds and lists their members. Economic and social organisation outside the state apparatus.
The benefits of guild membership - collaboration, shared information, autonomy. Same economic-history lane as the other shreni items.
Fertile plains, iron ore, forests and rivers behind Magadha's rise is economic geography. Not LO-78, because resources are treated as advantages, not as administered assets.

Iron weapons strengthening the army and iron ploughs funding it through a larger surplus is how a state built military power. The military clause of LO-78 carries the answer, which is why this differs from the purely geographical Magadha item.
